body: An adult lion has a broad chest, muscular shoulders, sandy-gold short fur, rounded ears and a long tail ending in a dark tuft. An adult male usually has a thick mane framing the face and neck; a lioness lacks the mane and has a slimmer outline. Lions walk on large padded paws with a measured, rolling gait, and often rest together in open grass under warm daylight. Their faces are calm but alert, with amber eyes and long whiskers. Nearby, quiet breathing, low contact grunts and the dry swish of grass are audible; a distant roar is deep and carrying.

A tiger is a large, solitary cat with a long, muscular body, a broad head and a heavy tail. Its orange coat carries irregular black vertical stripes over pale fur on the cheeks, throat, belly and inner legs. The stripe pattern continues onto its face and tail; individual patterns vary. It walks silently on broad, soft paws, shoulders rising and falling beneath the fur, then may pause to watch or sniff its surroundings. In dappled forest light, its coat shifts between bright orange and shadow. Calm sounds include breath, a soft chuff and leaves brushing its body.

An African elephant has a massive grey body, pillar-like legs, wide fan-shaped ears and a flexible trunk reaching nearly to the ground. Its skin is thick and deeply wrinkled, with sparse coarse hairs; some adults have curved ivory tusks. It walks with slow, surprisingly quiet steps on broad cushioned feet, while its trunk explores, gathers grass or sprays water. The ears flap loosely in the heat. In open savanna daylight, dust can settle into the skin folds. Low rumbles carry between elephants, with occasional airy breaths, footfalls and a louder trumpet when one calls.

A giraffe stands on very long legs beneath a sloping back and an exceptionally long neck. Its tan coat has large, irregular brown patches separated by pale lines; short hair covers the body, and a dark tuft tips the tail. Small skin-covered horns, called ossicones, rise between large ears above long-lashed eyes. It walks with both legs on one side moving nearly together, giving its stride a gentle sway. When reaching leaves, its dark, grasping tongue curls around them. In clear savanna light, expect soft hoof taps, leaf rustles and occasional snorts rather than constant calling.

A plains zebra is horse-shaped but stockier, with upright ears, a short stiff mane and a tail ending in a long hair tuft. Bold black and white stripes cover its body and legs, forming a distinct pattern on each animal. It stands alert in grassy plains, sometimes swishing its tail or grooming a nearby zebra. At a walk, its hooves land in a steady four-beat rhythm; at a trot, its head and mane bob lightly. Strong sunlight picks out the stripe contrast and a slight sheen on the short coat. Its calls are bark-like brays, alongside snorts and hoofbeats.

A long-tailed macaque is a compact monkey with brown-grey fur, a lighter underside, a mostly bare expressive face and grasping hands and feet. Its tail is long and slim, helping with balance rather than gripping branches. It moves on all fours along branches or the ground, then climbs with quick, deliberate handholds and short jumps. In a calm group, individuals sit close, inspect one another’s fur and glance around with bright, attentive eyes. Daylight catches the fine fur around their cheeks. Soft chatters, brief squeaks, leaf movement and light taps on branches fill the background.

A gorilla has a broad chest, powerful shoulders, long arms and dark, dense hair surrounding a mostly bare face, ears, hands and feet. An adult male may show a silver-grey saddle across his back. On the ground it usually knuckle-walks, placing curled fingers down as its body shifts in a steady, weighty rhythm. A relaxed gorilla may sit to pull leaves closer, chew slowly or watch others with a composed expression. Soft forest light reveals the hair’s texture and the contours of its brow. Expect rustling vegetation, quiet grunts, breaths and occasional low, resonant calls.

A brown bear has a heavy rounded body, a shoulder hump, small round ears and a short tail almost hidden by thick fur. Its coat ranges from light brown to dark chocolate, with longer guard hairs catching the light. It walks on the full soles of its broad feet, producing a slow, rolling gait; curved claws are visible beyond the toes. A calm bear may sniff the air, turn stones or forage among berries beside a stream. Its nose moves constantly as it investigates. Audible details include heavy breathing, soft huffs, pawfalls on soil and water moving over rocks.

A wolf is a long-legged, deep-chested canine with a broad muzzle, upright triangular ears, and a thick tail carried mostly low. Its dense coat mixes gray, brown, cream, and black, with lighter fur around the cheeks and underside. It walks in a steady, ground-covering trot, placing its paws neatly and keeping its body level; when alert, its ears lift and its gaze fixes on a distant sound. A calm wolf may sniff the ground or glance toward other wolves nearby. Its sounds include low whines, short barks, and a sustained, rising howl. In daylight, the outer guard hairs catch the light above the softer undercoat.

A fox is a small, slender canine with a pointed muzzle, large upright ears, narrow legs, and a long, bushy tail. A familiar red fox has rusty orange fur across its back, white on the throat and chest, and darker lower legs; colour varies among foxes. It moves with light, quiet steps, pauses with one forepaw raised, then turns its head sharply toward a sound. Its tail swings behind it for balance as it trots or makes a short, springy leap. Fine whiskers frame its muzzle, and its eyes appear bright in side light. Foxes can give brief barks, yips, and soft whines.

A deer has a lean body, long slender legs, large sideways-set eyes, and tall ears that swivel toward sounds. Its coat is short and smooth, usually some shade of brown with a paler throat and belly. In many species, adult males carry branching antlers, while females do not; antler size and shape vary. A deer walks on paired hooves with a careful, almost silent step, then bounds with long, elastic strides when moving quickly. At rest, it may lower its head to graze and lift it to listen, ears pointed forward. Hooves can click on hard ground, and its breathing is quiet.

A gazelle is a slim antelope with a compact body, very fine legs, a narrow face, and large dark eyes. Its short coat is sandy or warm brown above and white below, often divided by a darker stripe along each side. Many species have curved or ringed horns; their shape and whether females have them vary by species. It stands poised on small, paired hooves, ears turning independently as it watches its surroundings. A gazelle walks lightly, runs with swift, even strides, and may spring upward with all four feet briefly clear of the ground. Hooves make faint taps on firm soil; grazing is quiet.

A rabbit has a rounded body, long mobile ears, large side-facing eyes, a short cottony tail, and powerful hind legs much longer than its forelegs. Its fur is dense and soft, commonly brown, gray, white, or a mixture that blends with the ground. It sits with its back curved and nose twitching rapidly while whiskers brush nearby grass. When it moves, the front feet land first and the hind feet swing forward in a compact hop; quicker hops stretch its body low over the ground. Rabbit ears pivot toward small sounds. It is usually quiet, with faint snuffling and soft footfalls on dry leaves.

A squirrel is a small rodent with bright side-set eyes, rounded ears, grasping front paws, and a long tail covered in thick fur. Its coat may be gray, reddish brown, or sandy, often paler underneath. It travels in quick bursts: scampering along a branch, stopping abruptly, then climbing with its claws gripping bark. When it leaps, its body stretches between branches and its tail trails behind, helping it balance on landing. It can sit upright to hold a seed between its forepaws, rotating it as it nibbles. Claws make tiny scratches on bark; some squirrels give sharp chirps or chattering calls.

A hedgehog is a small, low-bodied mammal with a pointed snout, short legs, tiny rounded ears, and a back covered in stiff, cream-and-brown spines. Its face and belly have softer fur, and its dark nose moves constantly as it sniffs. It walks close to the ground with short, deliberate steps, rustling through dry grass or leaves. When uncertain, it may pause, tuck its head, and draw its spiny back into a rounded shape; when relaxed, its face and feet remain visible. Its sounds are quiet snuffles, breathing, and occasional soft grunts. Side light picks out the separate spines clearly.

A freshwater turtle has a broad, hard upper shell, a flatter lower shell, a small beaked head, four clawed feet with some webbing, and a short tail. The shell is part of its body, with curved plates that may be olive, brown, or dark green. On land it walks slowly, lifting one side at a time, its claws making faint taps on stone. In water it moves more smoothly, paddling its limbs in alternating strokes and steering with small adjustments of its feet. It may pause with only its eyes and nostrils above the surface. Turtles are generally quiet; movement may produce gentle splashes or shell contact sounds.

A tortoise has a high, domed shell with hard, polygonal plates in mottled tan, brown, or olive. Its head, thick neck, and four sturdy, scaly legs emerge beneath the shell; the feet are blunt and clawed, not flippers. It walks slowly, shifting its weight from side to side and placing each foot firmly on the ground. Its small eyes blink, and its beak-shaped mouth nips leaves without chewing motions like a mammal’s. It may pause or draw its head partly inward when approached. Usually quiet, it makes faint scrapes on gravel and soft rustles through dry grass in warm daylight.

A calm snake has a long, limbless body covered in small, overlapping scales that catch light with a subtle sheen. Its colour and markings vary by species, from sandy brown to olive or patterned grey. It moves in smooth sideways curves, pushing against stones, soil, or vegetation; its belly stays close to the ground. The head leads steadily while the body follows the same path. It may pause and flick its narrow, forked tongue to sample the air. It has no external ears or blinking eyelids. A moving snake is nearly silent, apart from faint brushing against leaves or grit.

A typical small lizard has an elongated body, four short legs with spreading, clawed toes, a distinct head, and a long tapering tail. Fine scales give its skin a dry, textured look; browns, greys, and olive tones often blend with stone or soil. It moves in quick bursts, its body flexing sideways as alternating feet grip the ground, then stops abruptly with its head raised. Its eyes track nearby movement, and its throat may pulse gently as it breathes. On a sunny wall or rock, the scales show tiny highlights. It makes little sound beyond light taps and scratches from its feet.

A crocodile has a long, heavy body, short strong legs, a muscular tail, and a broad, elongated snout. Dark olive or brown skin is covered in tough scales and raised, bony ridges; the underside is paler. Its eyes and nostrils sit high on the head, so they can remain above water while most of the body is submerged. On land it moves deliberately, lifting its belly slightly as the legs step. In water, the tail drives a smooth, quiet glide while the legs tuck close. A resting crocodile may lie motionless in sun. Water laps softly around it; low grunts are possible.

A frog has a compact body, broad head, prominent eyes, short front legs, and long, folded hind legs built for jumping. Its moist skin may be smooth or slightly bumpy, often green, brown, or mottled to match plants and mud. At rest it crouches low with its hind feet tucked beneath it. To jump, it extends both powerful back legs at once, then lands on its front feet before settling again. In water, its hind legs kick outward and back, with webbed feet helping it swim. Near reeds or a pond, it may blink and inflate its throat while making short croaks.

A parrot has a rounded head, a strong curved beak, upright posture, and gripping feet with two toes pointing forward and two back. Its feathers may be green, blue, yellow, red, or mixed, depending on the species, with a tail ranging from short and squared to long and tapered. It climbs branches or a perch using its feet and beak for balance, tilting its head to inspect things. In flight it beats its wings firmly, then may glide briefly. Feathers lie sleek when relaxed and fluff slightly during grooming. Its sounds include sharp calls, whistles, and, in some individuals, imitated speech.

A peacock is a male peafowl with a small crested head, vivid blue neck and chest, sturdy grey legs, and a long train of iridescent upper-tail feathers trailing behind the shorter true tail. Each train feather ends in a colourful eye-shaped marking. It walks with measured steps, its train brushing the ground. When displaying, it lifts and spreads the train into a broad fan, sometimes trembling the feathers so they shimmer and make a faint rustle. Its wings are rounded and can carry it in short, forceful flights up to a branch or wall. Its calls are loud, high, and slightly harsh.

An eagle is a large bird of prey with broad wings, a deep chest, a hooked beak, and powerful legs ending in curved talons. Plumage varies by species but is often layered brown or dark feathers, with a paler head, underside, or wing markings. When perched, it stands upright and turns its head in small, alert movements; its eyes face forward and outward to scan the surroundings. In flight, it holds its wings wide and steady, riding rising air in long circles with only occasional deep wingbeats. Feathers shift subtly in the wind. Its calls are clear whistles or high, repeated cries, depending on species.

An owl has a compact body, a broad head, large forward-facing eyes and a short hooked beak partly hidden by facial feathers. Its soft plumage is mottled brown, grey or cream, with fine bars and spots; some species have feather tufts, while others have a smooth, round head. It sits upright on a branch, gripping with curved talons, and turns its head far to either side while keeping its body still. Broad wings carry it on quiet, gentle beats. It blinks slowly, gives low hoots or short calls, and appears most naturally in dim evening light.

A flamingo is a tall wading bird with a slim body, exceptionally long legs, a long curved neck and a thick bill bent sharply downward. Its feathers range from pale blush to coral pink, with black flight feathers most visible when its wings open. It walks slowly through shallow water, often holding its neck in a loose S shape, then dips its head upside down to filter food with its bill. When resting, it may balance on one leg with its head tucked into its back feathers. Groups make nasal honks and murmurs beside bright, reflective water.

A duck has a rounded, buoyant body, a broad flat bill, short legs set far back and webbed feet. Plumage varies by breed and species: a familiar domestic duck may be white with an orange bill, while a mallard drake has a glossy green head and a brown female has finely patterned feathers. On land it waddles with a side-to-side sway; on water it glides smoothly, leaving a V-shaped wake while its feet paddle beneath the surface. It dips its head or tips its body forward to feed. Ducks make quacks, softer chuckles and splashing sounds around ponds and canals.

A swan is a large waterbird with a heavy oval body, a very long flexible neck and broad wings folded high along its back. Many familiar swans are white, with densely layered feathers and a dark or orange-and-black bill, depending on species. It glides across still water with little visible effort, pushing with large webbed feet below the surface; on land its walk is slower and heavier. It bends its neck to preen or feed underwater, and may lift its wings slightly while swimming. Sounds include soft grunts, hisses and, in some species, resonant calls. Light catches the fine texture of its feathers.

A goose has a sturdy, elongated body, a medium-long neck, a wedge-shaped bill and strong legs with webbed feet. Its feathers are usually grey, brown and cream in wild species, or sometimes white in domestic birds. It walks with deliberate steps and a gentle body sway, grazing with short pulls of its bill. On water it floats high and paddles steadily; in flight, broad wings beat firmly as geese often travel in a loose V formation. It holds its head alert and gives loud, nasal honks and quieter contact calls. Its feather layers are clearly visible in side light near grass or water.

A mother hen has a rounded body, layered feathers, a small comb above her beak and sturdy scaly legs. Several chicks stay close to her feet: they are palm-sized, round and covered in soft yellow, brown or striped down, with tiny wings and quick, thin legs. The hen takes short, bobbing steps, scratches the ground backward with one foot and pecks at small bits of food. Chicks hurry after her in uneven bursts, stopping to peck and sometimes tucking beneath her body. She gives low clucks and brief calling notes; the chicks answer with high, continuous peeps in a calm yard or garden.

A rooster stands taller and more upright than a hen, with a prominent red comb and wattles, a pointed beak, sturdy scaly legs and long, arched tail feathers. Its neck feathers are narrow and glossy; its colours may be copper, black, white or patterned, depending on breed. It walks with deliberate, high steps, bobs its head while pecking and occasionally flaps its wings, stirring loose feathers. To crow, it stretches its neck upward, opens its beak and gives a loud, rising call followed by a rough falling note. In daylight, iridescent green or blue highlights may show on dark tail feathers.

A turkey is a large, heavy bird with a broad breast, small bare head, short strong beak and thick legs. Its body feathers are layered brown, bronze or black in many birds, while domestic varieties may be white. Loose red skin hangs at the throat, and a soft fleshy snood rests above the beak. It walks with measured, weighty steps and pecks at the ground. A male may calmly fan his wide, banded tail, lower his wings and puff out his chest, making the feathers rustle. Turkeys make gobbling calls, clucks and soft purrs, often heard in a farmyard.

An ostrich is a very tall, flightless bird with a small head, long bare neck and powerful, mostly bare legs ending in two toes per foot. Its rounded body carries loose, shaggy feathers; males are usually black with white wing and tail feathers, while females are dusty grey-brown. It walks with a rolling stride and runs on long, springy steps, its small wings lifting slightly for balance. The eyes are large, with noticeable lashes, and the beak is short and flat. On open ground it pecks at plants and looks around alertly. Footfalls thud softly; it may hiss or make a low booming call.

A camel calf has a narrow face, long lashes, soft lips and outsized, slender legs beneath a compact, woolly body. In an Arabian setting it is usually a young one-humped dromedary; its hump begins as a small, low mound rather than a tall adult hump. Coat colours range from cream to sandy brown, often with fuzz around the neck and head. It stands and walks on broad, padded feet, swaying slightly as it learns to keep pace with its mother. It nuzzles her flank and stays close in a yard or open grazing area. Its calls are soft, nasal bleats and grunts.

A donkey has a sturdy, compact body, a straight-backed profile, long upright ears and a short mane that stands like a brush. Its coat is commonly grey or brown, with a lighter muzzle and belly; some have a dark stripe down the spine and across the shoulders. The tail ends in a tuft of long hair. Small, hard hooves make distinct clopping sounds on stone or packed earth. It walks steadily with short, deliberate steps, pauses to turn its ears toward sounds and lowers its head to graze. Its bray begins as a rough intake and rises into a loud, carrying hee-haw.

A mule is the offspring of a donkey and a horse. It usually has a horse-like, muscular body and longer head, paired with noticeably long donkey-like ears. Its mane is short, its tail carries long hair, and its coat may be brown, grey, black or chestnut. Its height varies, but its legs tend to look lean and strong above neat, hard hooves. It walks with measured, sure-footed steps, especially on uneven paths, and its hooves click against rock or pavement. At rest it shifts its weight and swivels its ears independently. Its call can mix a horse-like whinny with a rough donkey-like bray.

An adult cow stands broad-bodied on four sturdy legs, with a long muzzle, sideways ears and an udder beneath its belly. Beside her, the calf is much smaller and narrower, with fine legs, a rounded face and a soft, short coat. Their colours may be solid brown or black, or marked with irregular white patches. The cow walks slowly, her weight shifting from side to side; the calf follows in quicker, sometimes unsteady steps and may nuzzle beneath her to nurse. In a farmyard or grassy enclosure, they sniff the ground and chew calmly. The cow gives a deep moo; the calf answers more softly and higher.

A goat kid is a small, light-framed young goat with thin legs, a short raised tail and a soft coat that may be white, tan, brown, black or spotted. Its face is narrow, its eyes have horizontal pupils, and its ears may point outward or droop according to breed. Tiny horn buds can be visible, though some kids have none. It moves in quick, springy steps, making brief hops and stopping close to its mother. It noses at leaves, clothing hems or a feeding bowl without force. Its hooves tap sharply on hard ground, and its high, wavering bleats sound thinner than an adult goat’s.

A lamb is a young sheep with a rounded body, slim legs, a short muzzle and a coat of soft, tightly curled or wavy wool. It may be creamy white, brown, black or patchy, with a small face and ears that angle outward. Compared with a goat kid, it looks stockier and woollier and usually keeps its tail down. It walks in short, light steps, occasionally bounding on all four legs, then settles near its mother to graze or nurse. Wool catches warm sunlight around its outline, while small hooves make faint taps on firm soil. Its bleat is high, gentle and nasal.

A Persian cat has a compact body, short sturdy legs, small rounded ears and a very long, dense coat that forms a ruff around its neck. Its face is round, with large eyes, a short nose and a broad, soft-looking muzzle; the degree of facial flatness varies. Coat colours include white, cream, grey, black and patterned combinations. Its plume-like tail follows behind as it walks with quiet, unhurried steps. Indoors, it often sits with its paws tucked beneath its chest or stretches out on a cool floor. Fur shifts gently as it moves. Its sounds are soft meows, occasional purrs and faint pawsteps.

A lean domestic cat with a narrow waist, long tail, pointed ears and short fur, often tabby, ginger, black or white with dusty patches. Its paws land quietly and precisely as it steps along a pavement edge or slips beneath a parked car. It pauses to sniff, flicks its ears toward traffic and squints in strong midday sun. A wary cat keeps a little distance from passersby; a familiar one may approach with its tail raised. Expect soft meows, brief chirps and the scrape of claws on concrete. Warm light catches its whiskers against shopfronts and beige walls.

A German shepherd is a large, athletic dog with a long muzzle, upright triangular ears, a deep chest and a bushy tail carried low. Its dense double coat is often tan with a black saddle and mask, though solid black and sable coats also occur. At a walk, its long legs produce a smooth, ground-covering stride; when alert, its ears turn toward a sound and its head lifts. It may pant with its mouth open, sniff the ground or sit beside its handler. Breathing, collar jingles, nails clicking on tile and an occasional low bark are audible. Sunlight separates the glossy guard hairs from the softer undercoat.

A golden retriever is a medium-large dog with a broad head, soft hanging ears, a sturdy chest and a long, feathered tail. Its thick golden coat ranges from pale cream to deep gold, with longer, slightly wavy hair along the legs, chest and tail. It walks with an easy, even gait and often approaches familiar people with a loose body and wagging tail. When sitting, it may tilt its head toward a voice; after drinking, drops cling to the fur beneath its mouth. Expect gentle panting, nails tapping on a floor, collar sounds and occasional barks. Side light gives the layered fur a warm glow.

A Saluki is a tall, slender sighthound with a narrow head, deep chest, tucked waist and long legs. Its short, smooth coat may be cream, fawn, black or patterned; many have silky feathering on the ears, tail and backs of the legs, while smooth-coated Salukis do not. It stands lightly on compact paws, watching distant movement, then crosses open ground in long, elastic strides with its spine flexing. At rest it may fold its legs neatly beneath itself beside a handler. The dog is usually quiet; its paws make soft taps on hard ground, with light panting after exercise. Low sun outlines its fine coat.

A hamster is a small, round-bodied rodent with short legs, tiny rounded ears, glossy dark eyes and prominent whiskers. Fur may be golden, white, grey or mixed, depending on the kind; the tail is very short and usually hidden by the coat. It moves in quick starts and stops, sniffing bedding and gripping food with its front paws. Its cheek pouches can swell noticeably when it carries seeds. In a clean enclosure, it burrows into paper bedding, climbs low surfaces and runs in a suitably sized wheel. Sounds are subtle: bedding rustles, claws patter and the wheel turns with a soft hum. Gentle light reveals individual hairs.

A goldfish has overlapping reflective scales, round eyes and translucent fins that fan and fold as it swims. Colour ranges from orange and gold to white, red-and-white or dark patches. Body shape varies: common goldfish are streamlined with a single tail, while fancy varieties are rounder and often have paired tails. In a clear, spacious aquarium, it advances with small side-to-side tail beats, steers with its pectoral fins and hovers by making constant tiny adjustments. Its mouth opens and closes as water passes over the gills. The fish makes no noticeable voice; listen instead for filter water and faint surface ripples. Aquarium light flashes across its scales.

A butterfly has six thin legs, a slender body, two antennae with slightly thickened tips and four broad wings covered in fine coloured scales. Wing patterns vary by species, often showing spots, bands or dark borders that appear different when the wings close. It flies in a wavering path with repeated wingbeats and short glides, then lands lightly on a flower or leaf. At rest, it may slowly open and close its wings; a narrow, coiled feeding tube extends toward nectar. Butterfly wings make no audible flutter at ordinary distance. Soft daylight brings out their delicate texture, while a nearby breeze shifts both insect and flower.

A worker honeybee has a compact, fuzzy thorax, a banded brown-and-gold abdomen, six jointed legs, elbowed antennae and two pairs of clear wings. Its large compound eyes sit on either side of the head. In flight, rapidly beating wings create a steady, high buzz; the bee hovers briefly before settling on a flower. It walks over petals, probes with its mouthparts and gathers yellow pollen on its hind legs. It then lifts off, legs tucked beneath the body, and follows a purposeful path to another bloom. In warm daylight, fine hairs catch the light, while the moving wings appear as translucent blurs.

A worker ant is a tiny insect with a distinct head, narrow waist and rounded abdomen. Its hard body may be black, reddish brown or amber, with six jointed legs and two elbowed antennae that constantly probe the ground. Workers walk in quick, uneven steps, pausing to touch antennae with another ant or carry a crumb in their jaws. A close view shows a slight shine on the shell and fine texture along the legs. Ants often follow an irregular trail across soil, pavement or a kitchen ledge. They make no readily audible sound at ordinary camera distance.

A dragonfly has a long, slender abdomen, a compact chest, six thin legs and an oversized head dominated by two rounded compound eyes. Four transparent wings extend sideways, their delicate veins catching the light. Colours range from muted brown to vivid blue, green or red, depending on the species. It can hover nearly motionless, dart sideways, reverse direction and settle on a reed with its wings held open. Its legs tuck beneath the body during flight. Near a pond or irrigation channel, sunlight flashes across the wings; a close microphone may catch a faint wing rustle, but it is usually silent to people nearby.

A dolphin has a smooth, streamlined grey body, a rounded forehead, a short beak in many species and a curved dorsal fin. Two pointed flippers steer while the broad tail flukes beat up and down, not side to side. Its skin looks wet and reflective as it rolls through the surface, briefly exposing the blowhole on top of its head to breathe. Dolphins often travel together, surfacing in fluid arcs before slipping back beneath the water. Above water, a breath sounds like a quick puff amid splashes; underwater, they produce whistles and rapid clicks. Bright surface light ripples across their backs.

A whale is a large marine mammal with a smooth, tapered body, two flippers and broad horizontal tail flukes that drive it forward with slow up-and-down strokes. Shape, colour and size vary greatly by species: some are dark grey with pale patches, while others have a more uniform back. At the surface, its blowhole releases a forceful breath and a visible misty spout in cool air. It may roll, show a curved back, then lift its tail as it dives. Low light makes the wet skin gleam. Nearby listeners hear the breath and water washing aside; some species also make calls audible underwater.

A calm shark glides through water with a firm, streamlined body, pointed or rounded snout, visible gill slits behind the head and a prominent dorsal fin. Its pectoral fins spread outward for lift, while the uneven tail sweeps side to side to propel it forward. Many species have a grey or brown back and a paler underside; skin appears matte rather than slick at close range. It holds a steady course, making gentle turns without abrupt lunges. In clear water, shifting sunlight patterns pass over its back and the seabed. The shark makes no vocal sound; only water movement and distant underwater ambience are heard.

An octopus has a soft, rounded mantle, two alert eyes and eight flexible arms lined with suction cups. Its skin can shift colour and texture, appearing smooth one moment and subtly raised or mottled the next. It crawls over rock by placing and curling its arms, feeling along crevices with the cups. When swimming, it may gather its arms and pulse water through a funnel beneath the mantle, moving in a short, smooth burst. In shallow coastal water, rippled sunlight plays over its body as it pauses beside a rock. It has no vocal call; the scene sounds of water, bubbles and nearby marine life.

A jellyfish has a translucent, umbrella-shaped bell with soft trailing oral arms and, in many species, fine tentacles. Its outline may be clear, milky white, pink or faintly blue. The bell contracts and relaxes in slow pulses, pushing water backward, while currents carry much of its movement. Thin edges glow when sunlight filters through the water, revealing faint internal shapes without making the animal look solid. Several may drift at different depths, their trailing parts following the flow rather than swinging like hair in air. Jellyfish make no vocal sound; the audible scene is gentle water movement and distant bubbles.

A penguin is an upright seabird with a compact body, short legs set far back, a pointed beak and stiff, flipper-like wings. Most have a dark back and pale belly, though markings and size differ by species. On land it waddles with short steps, balancing with its flippers, and may slide on its belly over snow where conditions allow. Underwater it drives itself forward with strong wing strokes, steering with its feet and tail. Dense, short feathers look smooth from a distance and bead with water when it emerges. Colonies can be noisy with braying or chirping calls, footfalls and surf along the shore.

A polar bear has a long neck, small rounded ears, a tapered muzzle and a powerful body carried on four broad paws. Its dense fur looks white or cream, sometimes yellowish in warm light, with individual guard hairs visible along the shoulders. Black skin shows at the nose, lips and paw pads. It walks with a heavy, rolling gait, leaving wide prints in snow; in water it swims steadily with its front paws. A calm bear may sniff the air or turn its head slowly. Breathing, snorts and low huffs are more natural than constant roaring. Arctic daylight gives the fur cool blue shadows.

A giant panda is a stocky bear with a round head, short tail and thick, slightly coarse-looking fur. Its body is creamy white, with black ears, eye patches, shoulders and legs; the dark patches sit around the eyes rather than covering the whole face. It often sits upright with its hind legs forward, gripping bamboo stalks with its paws and chewing slowly. When walking, it moves on all fours with short, deliberate steps and a gentle body sway. Snuffles, soft bleats and the dry crack of bamboo are plausible sounds. Natural light reveals separate hairs along the edges of the black and white markings.

A kangaroo has a small head, tall mobile ears, short forearms, large hind feet and a thick, muscular tail extending behind its body. Its short fur is usually grey or reddish brown, with a paler chest and belly. At speed it hops on both hind legs together, the tail balancing each springing arc; while grazing slowly, it uses its forelimbs and tail for support. It pauses upright to look around, ears pivoting independently toward sounds. Quiet snorts, foot thumps and soft rustling in dry grass suit a calm scene. Strong sunlight picks out the contours of its hind legs and tail.

A koala is a compact tree-dwelling marsupial with a large black nose, round fluffy ears, short tail and dense grey fur over a pale chest. Its forepaws grip branches with strong curved claws and opposing digits; its hind paws brace against the bark. It climbs deliberately, shifting its weight before reaching for the next hold, and often rests curled against a fork in a eucalyptus tree. A calm koala blinks slowly or sniffs leaves before chewing them. Leaves rustle around it; occasional low grunts are possible, though a resting koala is often silent. Soft daylight shows the woolly texture of its coat.

A horse foal has a compact body, a short muzzle and notably long, slender legs with small hooves. Its coat may be bay, chestnut, black or grey, with soft hair and a short, wispy mane and tail. It stands close to its mother, flicking its ears and taking quick, curious looks at nearby movement. A young foal walks carefully, then breaks into a light, slightly uncoordinated trot; its hooves make small, crisp taps on firm ground. Soft nickers and breathing accompany a quiet paddock scene. Morning light catches the fine hair around its ears and muzzle.

An Arabian falcon is a streamlined bird of prey with a hooked beak, dark alert eyes, long pointed wings and strong yellow feet tipped with curved talons. Plumage varies by species, often combining brown or slate-grey upper feathers with a lighter, finely marked underside. At rest it stands upright on a falconer’s leather glove or a padded perch, turning its head sharply to follow movement. In flight, firm wingbeats alternate with smooth glides; feathers flex subtly in the wind. Its calls are sharp, repeated cries rather than a constant soundtrack. Desert light brings out the layered feather edges and the texture of traditional leather equipment.

On an Iraqi rooftop, keepers release small groups of domestic pigeons from simple coops with wooden perches, wire fronts and shaded openings. The birds have compact bodies, small heads and iridescent green or violet neck feathers; their plumage may be grey, white, brown or mottled. They launch with rapid, audible wingbeats, gather into a loose flock and circle above neighbouring roofs before settling with brief flared-wing landings. A keeper may watch from beside the coop, using familiar calls or a light whistle to guide them home. Wing flutters, coos and distant street sounds mix in the warm late-afternoon light.

The Arabian oryx is a pale, stocky antelope with a straight back, dark legs, a dark facial mask and two long, nearly straight horns on both males and females. Its short white coat reflects harsh sunlight; the neck and shoulders show faint sandy shading. It walks with measured steps across gravel plains and sparse desert scrub, then trots with a level body when moving faster. Its ears turn toward sounds, and it pauses to watch quietly. Hooves make dry, light clicks on stone; snorts are brief and soft. In low desert sun, its white flanks stand out against beige ground.

The Arabian wolf is a lean, long-legged canid, smaller and lighter-coated than northern wolves. Its coarse fur is sandy grey to brown, with a darker back, pale underside, pointed ears and a low, bushy tail. In rocky desert or dry hills, it walks at an economical trot, placing its narrow paws carefully among stones. It may stop, raise its ears and sniff the air before continuing. Its expression is alert rather than snarling. Footsteps are usually quiet; it can make short barks, whines or a thin, sustained howl. Twilight softens the contrast in its mottled coat.

A calm striped hyena has a sloping back, powerful shoulders, shorter hind legs and a long neck edged by a shaggy mane. Its coarse beige-grey fur carries narrow black stripes on the legs and body; the face has a dark muzzle and large upright ears. It moves with a steady, slightly rolling walk, nose near the ground as it investigates dry scrub or rocky ground. At rest, its mane lies relatively flat and its posture remains unhurried. Its feet scuff gravel softly; low grunts and brief nasal calls are more fitting than constant loud vocalising. Side light picks out the rough fur.

A golden jackal is a medium-sized canid with a pointed muzzle, upright triangular ears, slender legs and a bushy tail carried low. Its coat mixes tawny, grey and black-tipped hairs, with paler fur under the throat and belly. It trots lightly along field edges, reed margins or dry tracks, often pausing to look back or sniff a patch of ground. Its movements are quick but controlled, and its ears flick independently toward faint noises. Footfalls are soft on dirt; short yelps, barks and wavering calls can carry across open ground. Warm evening light brings out the tawny sides.

The fennec fox is a very small desert fox with exceptionally large upright ears, a short pointed muzzle, dark eyes and a full tail tipped in black. Dense, pale cream fur covers its body and even the soles of its feet. It moves in quick, light steps over sand, stopping suddenly to listen with ears angled in different directions. When calm, it sits low with its tail wrapped beside its paws or noses gently at the ground. Its calls are soft squeaks, whimpers and short barks; its padded feet barely sound on sand. Moonlight or cool dawn light gives the coat a silvery edge.

A jerboa is a small desert rodent with a rounded body, large eyes, long whiskers, short forelegs and greatly elongated hind feet. Its sandy coat is pale underneath, while a long thin tail ends in a dark-and-white tuft. It sits upright to survey open ground, then travels in sudden bouncing leaps, using its tail for balance and changing direction between landings. At rest, it may hold its tiny forepaws close to its chest. Sand makes only faint taps beneath its feet; any squeaks are quiet. Low-angle night lighting reveals the tail tuft and its long, delicate shadow.

A marsh water buffalo is a heavy, broad-bodied animal with dark charcoal skin, sparse hair, drooping ears and horns that sweep outward and backward. Its wide muzzle often looks wet, and mud dries in pale patches along its flanks. It walks slowly through shallow water, lifting each hoof against the drag of soft silt; when resting, much of its body may remain submerged. It blinks calmly and swishes its tail at flies. Water sloshes around its legs, reeds rustle, and it gives low grunts or breathy snorts. Iraqi marsh scenes may include reed beds, a narrow boat and a nearby herder.

A wild mountain goat in Kurdistan has a compact body, strong narrow legs and split hooves that grip broken rock. Its brown coat is lighter beneath, with a darker line along the back; adult males have a beard and long, ridged horns curving backward, while females are smaller with shorter horns. It climbs steep limestone slopes in deliberate steps, testing each foothold before shifting its weight, then pauses on a ledge with its head raised. Hooves click against stone, and brief nasal bleats carry in still air. Clear mountain light outlines the horns against ridges and sparse hillside shrubs.

A leopard is a muscular, medium-sized big cat with a broad head, rounded ears, thick paws and a long balancing tail. Its short golden coat carries dark rosettes, with solid spots on the face and legs and a pale belly. It walks quietly with rolling shoulders, then climbs using its forelegs and hooked claws. In calm scenes it pauses on a branch or moves through dry grass, ears turning toward faint sounds. Its calls include a rough, rasping cough and low growls. Dappled daylight makes the rosettes visible against bark, rock and grass.

A running cheetah is lean and long-legged, with a small head, deep chest, flexible spine and long tail. Its tan fur has separate black spots rather than rosettes; dark tear lines run from each eye toward the mouth. At speed, its back flexes sharply as the hind legs reach forward and the body stretches nearly horizontal between footfalls. The tail swings to help steer, while the paws grip dusty ground and scatter small puffs of sand. Breathing becomes rapid and audible during a sprint. In bright open grassland, its movement alternates between explosive strides and brief airborne moments.

A black panther is a melanistic big cat, commonly a leopard in African or Asian settings. It has a broad feline head, rounded ears, strong shoulders, large paws and a long tail. The coat looks black at a distance, but faint rosette markings appear where angled sunlight catches the short, glossy fur. It moves with a quiet, fluid walk, shoulder blades rising beneath the skin, and can climb a low tree with controlled pulls of its forelegs. Its eyes catch small highlights in shade. Soft footfalls, breath and occasional low, rasping calls suit a calm woodland scene.

A rhinoceros has a barrel-shaped body, short powerful legs, small eyes and ears that swivel independently. Its thick grey or brown-grey skin forms deep folds around the shoulders and legs and often carries dried mud. Depending on the species, one or two horns rise from the snout; they are solid keratin, not bone. It walks with a heavy, measured gait, its broad three-toed feet pressing shallow marks into soft earth. Quiet snorts, grunts and forceful breathing accompany grazing or resting near water. Strong side light reveals the skin’s rough texture and the horn’s worn surface.

A hippopotamus is enormous and barrel-bodied, with short stout legs, a broad square muzzle, tiny ears and eyes set high on the head. Its nearly hairless skin looks grey-brown and glossy when wet, sometimes showing pinkish areas around the face and folds. In water, most of the body stays submerged while the eyes, ears and nostrils remain visible. It moves slowly on land but pushes steadily along the riverbed underwater, surfacing with a splash and a puff of breath. Its calls are deep grunts and resonant wheezes. Muddy banks and warm, reflected daylight provide a natural setting.

A wildebeest migration appears as long, uneven streams of grey-brown antelope crossing open savanna. Each animal has a heavy front end, sloping back, dark mane, beard and curved horns; calves are smaller and lighter brown. The herd moves in a flowing mass rather than perfect rows, with individuals trotting, slowing and changing direction around patches of grass or shallow water. Hooves raise low clouds of dust in dry ground and make dull splashes at a crossing. Hoofbeats, nasal grunts and occasional bellows blend into a continuous sound. Wide daylight views show the herd stretching toward the horizon.

Meerkats are small, slender mammals with sandy-brown fur, darker bands across the back, black patches around the eyes and thin tails with dark tips. Their pointed snouts and small rounded ears are clear in close views. They scurry on short legs, dig with long foreclaws and often rise upright on their hind legs to look around, using the tail for balance. Several may gather near a burrow while others nose through dry soil for food. Their sounds include soft chirps, squeaks and sharper contact calls. Low sunlight picks out their fur against pale sand and sparse scrub.

A familiar ring-tailed lemur has a slim grey body, white underside, pointed muzzle, pale ears and dark patches around amber eyes. Its long, bushy tail has alternating black and white rings and is often held upright while walking. On the ground it moves on all fours with quick, light steps; between low branches it springs with its hind legs and catches itself with its hands and feet. Groups sit close together or groom quietly in warm sunlight. Their sounds range from soft clicks and purr-like calls to louder mewing notes. Fine fur catches light along the face and tail.

A three-toed sloth has a round, small head, a short snout, dark patches around its eyes, and shaggy gray-brown fur that can look faintly green in damp forest light. Its long limbs end in three curved claws on each foot. It usually hangs beneath a branch, gripping securely while its body sways slightly. Movement is exceptionally slow: one limb reaches, hooks onto wood, and takes weight before another lets go. On the ground it drags itself awkwardly rather than walking upright. It is generally quiet, though a nearby sloth may make a soft squeak or nasal call.

A red panda is roughly house-cat sized, with rust-red fur, a pale muzzle, white cheek markings, dark legs, pointed ears, and a long, bushy tail marked with faint rings. Its body is low and flexible, with short legs and furry paws that grip branches. It walks carefully along limbs, climbs headfirst down trunks by turning its hind feet, and often curls up with its tail across its face. While feeding, it holds bamboo stems between its forepaws and chews steadily. Small squeaks, twitters, and occasional breathy calls are more plausible than loud roars. Woodland shade softens its red coat.

A river otter has a long, streamlined body, short legs, a broad muzzle with pale whiskers, and a thick tail that tapers gradually to a point. Dense brown fur looks sleek and darker when wet, while the throat is often lighter. In water it glides with undulations of its back and tail, steering with webbed feet; on a bank it bounds with a rolling, low gait. It may surface with only its nose and eyes showing, then shake droplets from its coat. Otters chirp, whistle, and chatter softly. Along a quiet river, wet fur catches narrow highlights from the sky.

A beaver is a stocky brown rodent with a blunt head, small rounded ears, prominent orange incisors, and a wide, flat tail covered in dark scales rather than fur. Its hind feet are webbed; its smaller front paws can grasp twigs. On land it moves with a heavy, deliberate waddle, but in water its body floats low and its tail helps steer. It may carry a branch to the bank and strip bark with steady chewing motions. Water drips from its dense fur as it emerges. Expect quiet gnawing, splashes, and, when startled, a sharp tail slap on the water.

A raccoon has a rounded gray-brown body, a pointed pale muzzle, black fur around both eyes like a mask, and a thick tail with alternating dark and light rings. Its short legs end in narrow, dexterous paws with five visible fingers. It walks flat-footed with a rolling gait, climbs using its claws, and turns small objects over in its front paws. A raccoon near a stream may feel among stones or dip its paws in shallow water. Its coat looks coarse in side light, with fine guard hairs along the back. Sounds include soft chittering, snuffling, and occasional low growls.

A small insect-eating bat appears at dusk as a compact dark body between two broad wings of thin membrane stretched over elongated fingers. Its ears stand out when it passes close enough to see. The wings beat quickly, then pause briefly as it glides; its path bends and darts as it catches insects, rather than following a straight line. Against a fading orange or violet sky, the moving outline is clearer than its fur or face. Most echolocation is too high for people to hear, though a nearby bat may make faint, high squeaks. Wingbeats are usually nearly silent.

A house mouse is a small, light-bodied rodent with gray-brown fur, a pointed nose, rounded ears, black beadlike eyes, fine whiskers, and a long, nearly hairless tail. Its hind legs are slightly longer than its front legs. It moves in quick, low scurries, stopping abruptly to sniff before changing direction. The tail trails behind for balance, and the whiskers brush edges as it explores a wall or scattered crumbs. Under indoor light, its ears look thin and faintly pink. It makes tiny squeaks and soft scratching sounds; its footfalls are barely audible.

A guinea pig is a compact, oval-bodied pet rodent with a broad head, short legs, rounded ears, bright side-set eyes, and no visible tail. Its coat may be smooth, wiry, or arranged in swirls, often with patches of brown, white, and black. It walks close to the ground in short, quick steps and may make a sudden little hop when excited. Its front feet have four toes and its hind feet three. A calm guinea pig nibbles hay with rapid jaw movements and pauses to sniff. It communicates through clear whistles, soft purr-like rumbles, and quiet chirps.

A ferret has a long, flexible body, short legs, a small rounded head and a tapering tail. Its dense fur may be cream, brown or dark sable, often with a darker mask around bright eyes and a pink or dark nose. It moves close to the ground in quick, springy bounds, bending through narrow spaces and pausing to sniff with twitching whiskers. A relaxed ferret may roll onto its side or explore a soft blanket. Its claws make faint taps on hard floors; it may make soft chuckling sounds or squeak. Indoors, window light picks out the smooth sheen of its coat.

A chameleon grips a branch with mitten-like feet whose toes clasp from opposite sides. Its laterally flattened body has fine, pebbly scales, a curled prehensile tail and prominent eyes that can swivel independently. While it stays nearly still, patches of green, yellow, brown or darker tones shift gradually across its skin; the change is uneven, not a sudden match to the background. Mood, temperature and light can affect the colours. It advances with a slow, rocking step and watches its surroundings from the branch. Leaves may rustle faintly under its grip, but the animal itself is usually quiet. Daylight reveals the scales’ textured surface.

A small gecko rests flat against a plaster wall, with a broad head, large lidless eyes, splayed legs and wide toe pads. Its pale beige or grey skin may be mottled and slightly translucent in warm light; the tail extends behind it and can curve sideways. It walks vertically in short, precise bursts as microscopic structures on its toe pads grip the surface, then stops abruptly to watch. Thin toes lift and peel away one after another without leaving marks. Some house geckos make brief chirps or clicks, though a still one is silent. A nearby lamp casts a crisp, small shadow on the wall.

An iguana has a sturdy lizard body, a long muscular tail, strong clawed feet and a row of pointed scales running from its neck down its back. A green iguana may be leaf green, olive or brown, with a loose fold of skin beneath its throat and a round scale visible near the jaw. It rests on a broad branch with its legs spread for balance, then climbs using deliberate alternating steps; its tail follows as a counterbalance. It blinks slowly and turns its head to observe nearby movement. Claws scrape lightly on bark, while the animal is otherwise quiet. Sunlight sharpens each scale’s edge.

Seen from several metres away, a cobra has a long, smooth-scaled body lying in loose curves on sandy ground. Its colour may be tan, brown or nearly black, depending on the species. If alert, it can lift the front of its body and spread the ribs behind its head into a narrow hood; a calm cobra may keep its hood folded and move on. It travels in fluid sideways waves, its belly maintaining contact with the ground. Its dark eyes and small head show little facial expression. The snake is usually silent, with only a faint scrape over grit. Keep the viewpoint distant, with open space around it and soft daylight.

A desert scorpion stands low on eight jointed legs, with two pincers extending in front and a segmented tail curving above its back. Its hard outer shell may be sand yellow, amber or dark brown, with a slight shine where sunlight catches the joints. It walks slowly over firm sand, placing each foot carefully and pausing beside a pebble or patch of shade. The pincers open a little as it senses its surroundings; the tail stays curved without striking. Its movement is nearly silent, apart from a faint brush against dry grains. Low-angle light reveals shallow footprints and a small, sharply defined shadow.

An orb-weaving spider hangs from fine silk between a branch and a railing. Its body has a rounded abdomen, a smaller front section and eight long, jointed legs; colour and markings vary by species. It builds outward spokes first, then walks around them laying a spiral, touching each strand with its feet before securing new silk from spinnerets at the rear of its abdomen. The web flexes gently in a breeze but remains anchored at its edges. The spider moves with light, measured steps and makes no audible sound. Against shaded foliage, side light catches the silk as thin, bright lines.

A ladybug is a small, dome-shaped beetle with a smooth, glossy back split down the middle into two wing covers. Many are red or orange with black spots, though the number of spots and exact colours vary. Its short black legs carry it steadily along a leaf, while tiny antennae probe the surface. At the leaf’s edge, the wing covers lift apart and thin flight wings unfold beneath them; the beetle rises with a faint buzz, then folds the wings away after landing. It is otherwise quiet. Soft daylight reflects as a bright highlight on its curved shell, and the leaf bends only slightly under its weight.

A beetle has a compact body divided into head, thorax and abdomen, with six jointed legs and two antennae. Its hard front wings meet in a straight seam down the back, forming a shell over the thinner flight wings. Colour and size vary by species; a small garden beetle may be glossy black or brown, with a rounded or elongated outline. It walks in short, deliberate steps, gripping soil, leaves or a wall. To fly, it lifts the rigid wing covers and unfolds the wings beneath. Its footsteps are nearly silent; flight may produce a low buzz heard close up.

A grasshopper has a narrow, segmented body, a broad head with large side-facing eyes, short antennae and two powerful hind legs bent like springs. Green or straw-brown colouring blends with grass and dry stems. Its smaller front legs grip a stalk while it feeds on leaves. When startled, it pushes off suddenly, rises in a long arc and may open its wings for a brief flutter before landing. On the ground it shifts its legs in small, precise movements. Some species make a dry chirring sound by rubbing a hind leg against a wing, especially in warm, quiet fields.

A glowing firefly is a small, soft-bodied beetle with a dark, elongated body, six fine legs and short antennae. Its wing covers may have pale or reddish edges. The light comes from an area near the end of the abdomen, not from its eyes or wings. At dusk, a flying firefly traces a slow, uneven path above grass or shrubs, flashing a small yellow-green point; another may glow or flash while resting on a leaf. The light is gentle rather than a beam and is easiest to see against a dark background. Fireflies make no noticeable call; wingbeats are faint at close range.

A moth near a lamp has a soft, often furry body, two antennae and four wings dusted with fine scales. Its wings may be grey, tan or brown with subtle bands that show clearly when it rests flat against a wall. Around a bright porch bulb, it flies in irregular loops, sometimes passing close to the light, drifting away, then settling on the nearby wall or shade. Its wings beat rapidly but without the steady path of a bird. The moth itself is usually silent; a faint papery flutter may be heard if it brushes the lamp cover. Warm light casts a small moving shadow behind it.

A hummingbird is a tiny bird with a slender pointed bill, compact body, short neck and wings that blur during flight. Depending on species, its feathers may look green or bronze until sunlight catches an iridescent patch on the throat or head. It hovers in front of a flower, making minute adjustments with its tail, then darts quickly to another bloom. Its wing joints allow it to move backward as well as forward. A soft, rapid wing hum accompanies hovering, with occasional thin chips or squeaks. In a garden in the Americas, it may pause on a narrow branch between feeding visits.

A house sparrow is a small, round-bodied bird with a short, thick seed-cracking bill, brown wings, a greyish underside and sturdy pinkish legs. Males have a grey crown and black throat patch; females are plainer brown with a pale eyebrow. It moves on the ground in quick hops, pausing to tilt its head toward crumbs or seeds, then flies in a direct, slightly undulating line. Several may gather near a courtyard, pavement café or garden hedge. Their calls are short, repeated chirps and cheeps rather than a long melody. Sunlight picks out warm brown feather edges; in shade, the markings look softer.

A crow is a medium-sized, solidly built bird with a strong straight bill, dark eyes and broad wings. A black crow’s feathers can show a blue or violet sheen in direct sunlight, while looking nearly flat black in shade. It walks with measured steps, sometimes making a small hop, and turns its head to inspect the ground. In flight, its wings beat steadily between short glides, and its tail spreads slightly when it turns or lands. Its familiar call is a loud, rough caw, often repeated from a rooftop, tree or overhead wire. It may quietly forage alone or alongside other crows.

A Eurasian magpie is a black-and-white bird with a notably long, tapering tail and a stout dark bill. Its head and chest are black, its shoulder patches and belly are white, and sunlight brings green or blue iridescence to its wings and tail. It walks across grass with alert, deliberate steps, lifting its tail as it changes direction. In flight, rounded wings flash white patches beneath the darker feathers, followed by a glide toward a branch or wall. Its voice is a quick, harsh chattering call with several clacking notes. In gardens and parks, it often pauses upright to watch its surroundings.

A hoopoe is a slim, warm cinnamon-brown bird with a long, thin bill curved downward. Its rounded wings and tail carry bold black-and-white bands. A fan-shaped crest rises above its head when it is alert, then folds flat. On Iraqi lawns, farm edges and open ground, it walks in short steps, probing soil for insects and pausing to look around. Its flight is undulating, with broad wingbeats and brief glides. Its repeated call sounds like a soft, hollow “hoo-poo-poo.” In daylight, the striped wings flash clearly against dusty earth.

A common kingfisher is a compact bird with a large head, a long straight pointed bill and very short legs. Its back flashes electric blue and turquoise; the cheeks and belly are orange, with a white throat patch. It waits upright on a low reed or branch above still water, then drops headfirst to catch a small fish and returns to its perch with quick, direct wingbeats. It may hover briefly before diving. Its call is a sharp, thin whistle, often heard as it streaks past. Sunlight makes the blue feathers gleam against dark water.

A grey heron stands tall among Iraqi marsh reeds, with long dark legs, a straight yellowish bill and a slender neck that folds into an S shape. Its body is grey, with a pale head and neck marked by dark streaks; black plumes trail from behind the eyes. It waits almost motionless in shallow water, then makes one precise forward jab for a fish. Walking is slow and deliberate. In flight, broad wings beat steadily while the neck stays tucked and the legs extend behind. Its voice is a harsh, croaking “fraank,” especially when disturbed.

A great white pelican is a very large, heavy-bodied waterbird with pale white feathers, black flight feathers and a long yellow-orange bill. A flexible throat pouch hangs beneath the bill and stretches when it scoops up fish and water. On Iraqi wetlands it floats high, paddling with broad webbed feet, or joins other pelicans in a loose line on the water. It drains water from the pouch before swallowing a fish. Takeoff requires a running patter across the surface; in flight its broad wings carry it on slow beats and long glides. It is mostly quiet, with low grunts near others.

A white stork stands on a wide, untidy platform of dry sticks atop a pole, roof or tall structure. It has a white body, black flight feathers, long red legs and a long straight red bill. The nest is broad and shallow, with finer twigs and grass near the centre. The bird steps carefully around the rim, rearranging a twig or lowering itself over chicks or eggs. Its long wings open with slow, powerful beats before it lifts away. Adult storks are largely silent; pairs make a rapid wooden clatter by tapping their bills together.

A griffon vulture circling high overhead looks broad-winged and heavy, with a short tail, a small pale head and a pale neck ruff. Up close its body is sandy brown, while darker flight feathers edge the long wings. It rides rising warm air with wings fully spread, turning in wide, steady circles without flapping much. The wing tips separate into visible finger-like feathers; slight tilts of the wings tighten or widen the circle. Against bright Iraqi sky it may appear almost motionless until it banks. It is usually silent in flight, though it can hiss or grunt when close to other birds.

A hawk diving from a perch has a compact body, a hooked bill, strong feathered shoulders and yellow legs ending in curved talons. Brown or grey upper feathers contrast with a paler, often streaked underside. It leans forward, pushes off and drops in a steep, controlled glide, drawing its wings partly back before opening them to brake and turn near the ground. Its tail fans to steer; the dive is swift but not a perfectly vertical fall. Wingbeats make a brief rush of air, and some hawks give a thin, high “kree” call. Keep the scene calm, without contact or injury.

A barn owl has a pale, heart-shaped face with dark eyes, a small hooked bill and no ear tufts. Its back is mottled buff, grey and white; its chest and long legs are pale. At dusk it flies low over fields or the edge of a marsh on broad, rounded wings, alternating soft wingbeats with short glides. Fine feather edges make the flight unusually quiet. When perched, it stands upright and turns its head to listen, sometimes swaying gently. Its voice is a drawn-out, raspy screech or hiss, not the rounded hoot often associated with other owls.

An African grey parrot has a compact body covered in finely scalloped grey feathers, a pale bare face around bright eyes, a heavy curved black beak and a short scarlet tail. It grips a wooden perch with two toes forward and two back, shifting its weight and tilting its head toward a familiar person. Its beak opens in small, precise movements as it imitates a few human words, whistles or household sounds; the voice can sound surprisingly clear but uneven. Soft feather rustles and little clicks accompany its speech. Indoors, natural window light shows the layered texture of its feathers.

A budgie is a small, slim parrot with a rounded head, short hooked beak and a long, tapering tail nearly as long as its body. Pet birds are often green and yellow or blue and white, with fine dark bars across the head and wings. A fleshy cere surrounds the nostrils above the beak. It hops sideways along a perch, grips with two toes forward and two back, and flies in quick bursts with shallow wingbeats. Budgies chatter in rapid, high-pitched chirps and make softer contact calls. In a home cage, they climb wire bars and turn their heads alertly toward people.

A singing domestic canary is a small finch with a rounded body, neat conical beak, slender pinkish legs and a short, slightly notched tail. Many are bright yellow, though some have paler or darker feather patches. Perched on a thin branch or cage bar, it lifts its head, opens its beak and gives a flowing series of clear whistles, trills and quick warbles. Its throat pulses with the notes while the rest of its body stays fairly still; it may pause, blink and begin again. Daylight catches the fine feather edges, and faint claw taps sound when it changes perch.

topic: pigeons taking off from a square
body: Street pigeons stand close together on stone paving, their plump grey bodies marked with dark wing bars and iridescent green-purple neck feathers. Some are brown, white or mottled. When the group takes off, birds crouch, push hard with pink feet and beat pointed wings rapidly, rising at slightly different angles rather than as one solid shape. A brief rush of fluttering wings and scattered coos fills the square. Their shadows sweep across paving joints and low walls as they circle; individual birds bank by tilting their bodies and spreading their tails. People nearby may pause or glance up.

topic: racing pigeons returning to a roof
body: Homing pigeons approach a rooftop loft as small moving silhouettes, then show grey or blue-grey bodies, dark wing bars, glossy neck feathers and narrow leg bands. They circle once or twice, bank with one wing lower and slow by lifting their bodies and spreading their tails. Rapid wingbeats give way to a short flutter as pink feet reach for the roof edge or landing board. Claws tap on tile or wood; quiet coos follow as the birds fold their wings and walk toward the loft entrance. Rooftop tanks, parapets and nearby buildings give a familiar urban setting without obstructing their flight.

A flock of greylag geese crosses an open sky in a loose V, each bird separated from the next by visible air. They have broad grey-brown wings, pale underparts, long necks and orange bills. Their strong wingbeats look steady but are not perfectly synchronized; the two arms of the V stretch and shorten as individuals adjust position. A bird near the front may drop back while another moves ahead. Repeated nasal honks carry across the landscape, sometimes overlapping. Against low sunlight, the wings alternate between bright undersides and darker silhouettes as the flock passes over fields or water.

A gentoo penguin colony spreads across a rocky coastal slope, with dozens of upright birds showing black backs, white fronts, white patches above the eyes, orange-red bills and pink-orange feet. Adults stand roughly knee-high to an adult person. They waddle with short steps, balancing with their stiff flippers; on uneven ground they stop and lean before stepping again. Some sit beside shallow pebble nests while others face the sea. The colony sounds busy with braying calls, softer chirps and feet scraping gravel. Damp feathers catch a cool sheen in overcast light, while individual birds leave clear gaps between neighbouring nests.

A harbor seal has a rounded, streamlined body with a short neck, mottled grey or tan fur, large dark eyes, prominent whiskers and no visible external ear flaps. On a quiet beach or low rock, it rests with its front flippers tucked near its sides and its hind flippers extended behind. It moves awkwardly on land by flexing its body and sliding forward, but swims smoothly with side-to-side strokes of its hindquarters. It raises its head to look around, blinking and twitching its whiskers. Soft grunts or snorts mix with the wash of water; wet fur glistens in diffuse coastal light.

A sea lion has a smooth, streamlined body, a broad chest, a doglike muzzle with long whiskers, and small visible ear flaps. Its short, wet fur looks dark brown or tan and catches bright highlights. Long front flippers propel it through water; on land it rotates its hind flippers forward and walks with a rolling, four-flipper gait. It may lift its head, blink, and sniff while resting on coastal rocks or a sandy shore. Calm sea lions bark in short, hoarse bursts and make soft grunts. Water drips from their whiskers after they surface.

A walrus is massive and barrel-shaped, with wrinkled brown or pinkish-brown skin, sparse coarse hair, a broad whiskered muzzle, and two long ivory tusks pointing down from the upper jaw. Its small eyes sit above thick folds of skin. In cold coastal water it swims with broad flippers; on shore its heavy body heaves forward in slow, rolling movements. A calm walrus rests among others on ice or a rocky beach, occasionally raising its head or brushing its whiskers. It makes deep grunts, snorts, and hollow bell-like calls. Wet skin gleams in pale Arctic light.

An orca jumping from the sea has a glossy black body, a white underside, oval white patches behind the eyes, and a gray saddle behind the tall dorsal fin. Its powerful tail drives it upward; the curved body may clear the surface before gravity pulls it back down. Broad paddle-shaped flippers spread slightly as it twists. The landing throws up a wide sheet of white spray and a deep splash, followed by fizzing bubbles. Between jumps, a calm orca surfaces smoothly to breathe with a forceful, airy exhale. Sunlight flashes across wet skin against open water.

A manta ray has a broad, flattened body shaped like a diamond, with pointed winglike pectoral fins, a dark upper surface, and a pale underside. Two fleshy cephalic fins frame its wide forward-facing mouth; a slender tail trails behind without a stinger. It glides underwater by slowly flapping its large fins, banking smoothly rather than darting. Near plankton-rich water, it may roll or turn while feeding. Its movement is silent underwater, apart from surrounding water sounds. Filtered sunlight ripples over its back, while divers or reef fish provide scale for its several-metre wingspan.

A sea turtle has a rounded, streamlined shell patterned with large scutes, a small beaked head, and four flippers. The front flippers are long and powerful; they sweep downward and back to drive the turtle through water, while shorter rear flippers steer. Olive, brown, or greenish colours vary by species, with a lighter underside. A calm turtle glides between slow strokes, surfaces to breathe, then slips underwater again. It is usually quiet; only a brief breath and soft water sounds are audible. Sunlight makes wavering patterns across its shell above sand, seagrass, or reef.

A clownfish is a small, oval-bodied reef fish, commonly bright orange with three vertical white bands edged in black. Its fins flutter rapidly as it hovers and makes short, darting movements among an anemone’s many flexible tentacles. The tentacles sway with the current and close around the fish without trapping it. A clownfish may peek out, retreat, and emerge again while remaining close to its shelter. Underwater there is no audible call from the fish; faint reef and water sounds fill the scene. Clear tropical light reveals fine scales, translucent fin edges, and the anemone’s soft texture.

A starfish, or sea star, usually has five thick arms radiating from a central disc, though arm number and shape vary by species. Its upper surface may be orange, red, tan, or purple, with a rough texture of tiny bumps or spines. Beneath each arm, rows of small tube feet grip rock and pull it forward so slowly that movement is barely noticeable. It may rest on wet sand or cling to a tide-pool rock as water washes around it. The animal makes no audible sound; gentle surf and trickling water provide the sound. Its damp surface catches small highlights.

A beach crab has a low, hard shell, two jointed claws, and four pairs of walking legs extending sideways. Its sandy brown, gray, or mottled colouring blends with damp shore sand. Alert eyes on short stalks face outward as it pauses, then scuttles sideways in quick bursts, leaving small tracks. A calm crab may lift a claw to inspect food or retreat toward a shallow burrow when a wave approaches. Its feet make faint taps on firm sand; nearby surf is much louder. Low coastal sunlight picks out the shell’s edges and the wet sheen on its claws.

A live clawed lobster has a long, segmented body under a hard, mottled olive-brown shell, not the bright red of a cooked lobster. Two unequal claws extend in front of its small walking legs; long antennae sweep independently above dark eyes on short stalks. Its broad tail curls sharply under the body when startled. On a wet dock or in a seafood tank, it walks slowly with a slight rocking motion, claws held forward. The shell catches small, hard highlights under overhead light. Its legs make faint taps against glass or stone, while moving water provides most of the sound.

A common carp in the Tigris has a thick, deep body, olive-brown back, bronze flanks and pale belly. Large overlapping scales reflect brief flashes of light through the river’s cloudy green-brown water. Its long dorsal fin lies close to the back, and short whisker-like barbels sit beside its fleshy mouth. It swims with slow side-to-side sweeps of the tail, occasionally dipping its head to feed near the silty bottom. Near a quiet riverbank, reeds and reflected buildings waver on the surface. Underwater it is nearly silent; at the surface, a turn makes a soft splash and spreading rings.

A koi pond is a shallow-looking garden pool with dark water, stone or tiled edges, and several broad-bodied ornamental carp visible beneath the surface. Their white, orange, red and black patches have crisp or softly feathered boundaries; each fish has a single dorsal fin and a tail that sweeps steadily from side to side. They gather near the edge when someone approaches, opening round mouths at the surface without leaping. Sunlight makes moving ripples slide over their backs and across the pond floor. A small pump or waterfall murmurs continuously, with occasional soft gulps and splashes among the fish.

A dog playing fetch fixes its gaze on a thrown ball, accelerates across grass or packed earth, and bounds with a rolling, four-legged gait. Its ears and loose fur bounce slightly behind each stride; its tail balances turns. It slows before the ball, lowers its head and picks it up gently with its jaws, then trots back toward the person who threw it. On dusty ground, paws kick up small, brief puffs; on grass, the footfalls are muffled. Panting, collar jingles and an occasional excited bark accompany the movement. The dog looks alert and eager, with relaxed body language.

A wet dog plants its paws apart and begins a rapid shake at the head. The twist travels down its neck, torso and tail in a visible wave, while the skin and coat lag behind and whip from side to side. Water flies outward in fine droplets and larger beads, catching light for an instant before falling onto the floor or ground. Long ears flap broadly; a short coat makes the body’s twisting motion easier to see. The shake lasts only a second or two, ending with a small head flick. It makes a brisk flapping sound, followed by droplets pattering nearby.

A sleeping puppy curls on its side or tucks its nose near its hind legs, making a compact shape on a blanket or shaded floor. Its paws look slightly oversized beside its small body; soft fur rises and falls with steady breathing. Closed eyelids may twitch, and an ear or paw may make a tiny, brief movement without the puppy waking. The muzzle rests against fabric, and the jaw stays loose. Gentle window light shows fine hairs around the ears and the rounded pads of a relaxed paw. The scene is quiet apart from faint breathing, a sleepy sigh or fabric rustling when it shifts.

A cat stalking a small toy lowers its body close to the floor, hindquarters slightly raised and weight shifting carefully between padded paws. Its head stays level, eyes fixed on the toy, with ears pointed forward or turning toward a faint sound. Whiskers angle ahead as it advances in short, nearly silent steps. The tail may hold still with only its tip twitching. Before a playful pounce, the hind legs compress and the cat makes a quick, low spring, landing with its front paws around the toy. Claws may catch lightly on carpet; a bell or crinkly toy supplies the clearest sound.

A cat stepping or jumping down from a modest height first looks at the landing spot, then pushes off with its hind legs. In the air its flexible spine adjusts its posture and its tail shifts for balance. The front paws reach toward the ground first, followed closely by the hind paws; the legs bend on contact to absorb the impact. The body briefly crouches, then rises as the cat walks on. Fur moves slightly with the landing, especially along the belly and tail. On tile, the paws make light taps; on a rug, the landing is almost silent. A secure, unobstructed surface keeps the movement natural.

A small kitten has a round face, oversized ears, short whiskers, soft fine fur and paws that look large beside its slim legs. On a clean floor, it crouches with its belly low, then bats a loosely wound ball of yarn with one paw. The ball rolls unevenly, trailing a strand that slides across the floor. The kitten hops sideways, pins the yarn briefly and releases it, its tail lifted for balance. Soft paw taps, a faint rustle of fibers and an occasional tiny mew are audible. Window light picks out individual hairs and the yarn’s twisted texture.

An untacked horse stands in a broad patch of dry, loose sand. It lowers its head, folds its front legs and settles onto one shoulder before rocking onto its back. Its heavy barrel turns in slow, uneven surges while all four legs lift and flex above it. Sand shifts beneath its weight and dust clings to its short coat and mane. The horse rolls back onto its side, pushes itself upright and gives a whole-body shake that scatters fine grains. Expect dull hoof scrapes, sandy shuffling and a forceful snort.
